newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST - French Q2 GDP seen down 0.2-0.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - French Q2 GDP seen down 0.2-0.4 pct.

text.p: French GDP figures due at 0645 GMT on Wednesday are expected to show the economy shrank between 0.2 percent and 0.4 percent in the second quarter from the first quarter, economists said on Monday.

The fall in output, slowed by a sharp decline in private consumption, follows a strong 1.2 percent first-quarter expansion, which economists said was a reaction to the very weak fourth quarter of 1995.
"We still have to look at Q2 in light of what happened in Q1," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
They said the economy would continue to seesaw in reaction to last winter's strikes, with the third quarter showing firm growth of about 1.0 percent but the fourth producing only anaemic expansion.

Williams and other economists said the expected decline in second-quarter GDP would unsettle French financial markets in coming weeks but as long as the drop did not exceed about 0.4 percent, market reaction would probably not be too severe.
"This negative second quarter is likely to leave a bad impression in the markets for a long time," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
But he said the economy was performing better in September, and the second half of 1996 should be better than the first.
"September should be a good month, but we won't have any news of this until mid-October."
A sharp decline in private consumption was the main reason for the decline in second-quarter GDP, economists said. They predicted consumption fell by one percent in the quarter.
The drop was seen as a reaction to a sharp 2.4-percent consumption rise last quarter. It was also partly due to persistent weak consumer confidence, hit with continued high unemployment.
Stocks were expected to contribute about 0.5 percent to second-quarter GDP growth while a slightly smaller trade surplus subtracts about 0.3 percent, analysts predicted.
Overall investment was expected to rebound, Lehman Brothers economist Jane Edwards said.
Economists said the economy would grow in the third quarter, but it was unlikely the strong rebound the government is predicting for the second half would materialise.
"The Q2 GDP number will be old news," said JP Morgan economist David Naude. "The question is will the strong rebound the government expects materialise?
"My answer is no," he said. "The third quarter is doing better, but we're not expecting a sustained strong recovery."
The government forecasts 1996 growth of 1.3 percent.
